# Session 6: Protein Structure

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Tense and relaxed

> Haemoglobin walks into a bar. The bartender says: "You look tense."
>
> Haemoglobin: "Give me some oxygen and I'll relax."
:::

## Learning goals

By the end of this session you should be able to:

- describe the four levels of protein structure, using haemoglobin, and
  name the computational task that belongs to each;
- represent a structure as coordinates, as a distance map and as a
  contact map, and explain what each makes easy to see;
- explain the difference between a sequence alignment and a structure
  alignment, and why structure is often more conserved than sequence;
- interpret RMSD and TM-score, and explain at a conceptual level how
  DALI and Foldseek compare structures;
- explain why a single PDB entry is not necessarily "the" structure of a
  protein;
- state secondary-structure prediction as a supervised learning problem:
  what goes in, what comes out.

The question for this session is: **what information about a protein is
contained in its sequence, what becomes visible only in 3D, and how can
computers connect the two?** Sessions 3–5 worked with sequences,
retrieving them, aligning them and searching for families. In Session 3
you also found structures, but only as *database records* (a PDB entry,
an AlphaFold model). In this session the structure itself becomes the data. Its
coordinates can be turned into distances, secondary structure, domains
and interfaces, and compared with other structures. The course's globin
thread continues as well. In Session 3 you looked up *HBB*'s
identifiers, in Session 4 you aligned globin sequences and in Session 5
you searched for the globin family, and now you compare globin
structures.

## Sequence becomes structure {#sec-s06-levels}

### Four levels, four computational tasks

A protein starts as a **polypeptide chain**, a linear polymer of amino
acids, which folds into a 3D shape. Structural biology describes the
result at four levels, and in this course each level comes with its own
computational problem:

| Level | What it is | Computational task | Where in the course |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary** | the amino-acid sequence | alignment, BLAST, profiles | Sessions 3–5 |
| **Secondary** | local backbone shapes: α-helix, β-strand, coil | prediction from sequence | Sessions 7–11 |
| **Tertiary** | the 3D fold of one chain | structure comparison, prediction | this session; Session 12 |
| **Quaternary** | several chains packed together | interfaces, complexes | this session; Session 12 |

: The four levels of protein structure and where they appear in the course. {#tbl-s06-levels}

- An **α-helix** is a coil held together by hydrogen bonds between the
  backbone N-H and C=O groups of residues four apart. A **β-sheet** is
  built from extended **β-strands** that are hydrogen-bonded edge to
  edge. Everything else is called **coil**. Programs such as DSSP assign
  these labels from the coordinates of a solved structure.
- The tertiary fold is held together mainly by the **hydrophobic
  effect** (non-polar side chains bury themselves away from water),
  together with hydrogen bonds, electrostatic interactions and van der
  Waals contacts.
- Many proteins work as a single chain, while others assemble into
  complexes of two to hundreds of chains.

### Haemoglobin: all four levels in one protein

Haemoglobin is a **heterotetramer** of two α-globin chains (141
residues) and two β-globin chains (146 residues; β-globin is *HBB*, this
course's running example since Session 3). Each chain folds on its own
and carries an oxygen-binding haem group. Using PyMOL's
secondary-structure algorithm (`dss`), the notebook computes that one β
chain is **118 of 146 residues (80.8%) α-helix and 0% β-strand**. The
PDB entry's own annotation, which Session 7 uses, gives 117 helical
residues, because the two methods differ slightly in where exactly a
helix ends.

![PDB entry `2HHB`, human deoxyhaemoglobin: two α chains (blue/cyan),
two β chains (salmon/pink), four haem iron atoms (orange spheres).
Rendered from the real structure with PyMOL.](figs/session06-hemoglobin-tetramer.png){#fig-session06-hemoglobin-tetramer width=85%}

### Does the sequence determine the structure?

Whether a computer can predict a structure at all depends on how much of
it the sequence determines. In the 1960s Christian Anfinsen
showed that ribonuclease, unfolded in the test tube, refolds into its
active shape on its own once the denaturant is removed. For many small
globular proteins, then, the sequence contains enough information to
specify the native fold under the right conditions, and this principle
is what makes structure prediction possible. It is not a law for every
protein, however. Some proteins need chaperones to fold efficiently,
many need a ligand, cofactor or binding partner, some switch between
alternative states (haemoglobin itself, below), and **intrinsically
disordered** regions have no single fold.

Two kinds of interaction build a fold. **Local** interactions, between
residues close in sequence, form secondary structure. The hydrogen bonds
of an α-helix, for example, connect residues $i$ and $i+4$.
**Long-range** interactions, between residues far apart in sequence but
close in space, pack the helices and strands into a tertiary structure.
Local structure can therefore be partly guessed from a short window of
sequence (Session 7), whereas long-range structure cannot, which is why
tertiary-structure prediction is so much harder.

### A structure as a matrix: distance and contact maps

A structure file is a list of atomic coordinates, but coordinates are
not always the most useful representation. An alternative is the
distance between every pair of residues, which for a chain of $L$
residues gives an $L \times L$ **distance map**. Thresholding the
distance map gives a **contact map**, with 1 where two residues are
close (here, Cβ atoms within 8 Å) and 0 elsewhere. Unlike coordinates,
both maps stay the same however the protein is rotated or moved, so two
structures can be compared without first superimposing them.

![Three representations of β-globin (2HHB, chain B). Left: the 3D
structure, coloured from the N-terminus (blue) to the C-terminus (red).
Middle: the distance map. Right: the contact map, with the eight
α-helices of the PDB file as red bars. The band along the diagonal is
each helix in contact with itself (local interactions); the
off-diagonal stripes are helices packed against each other (long-range
interactions).](figs/session06-hbb-distance-map.png){#fig-session06-hbb-distance-map width=100%}

This representation returns twice later in the course. First, an $L
\times L$ map looks like an image, which is why image-processing
networks (CNNs, Session 10) turned out to be good at predicting
contacts. Second, coevolution, contact prediction and AlphaFold's "pair
representation" (Session 12) all work on residue-pair information like
this.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Representations

The same protein can be represented as a sequence, a profile (Session
5), a set of coordinates, a distance or contact map, or a learned
embedding (Session 11). The choice of representation determines which
patterns are easy to see and, later in the course, which patterns a
model can easily learn.
:::

### Looking at structures: PyMOL

To look at a structure yourself, you need a molecular viewer.
[PyMOL](https://pymol.org/) is, with ChimeraX, one of the two most
widely used, and its open-source version is free. It loads a structure
directly from the PDB and shows it as **cartoon** (secondary structure
as ribbons and arrows, as in the figures above), as **sticks** (every
bond, useful for a side chain or ligand) or as **spheres** (every atom,
useful for packing). It also measures distances and angles directly from
the coordinates. This session's lab uses PyMOL hands-on, and the notebook
drives the same program from Python, without a window, so that its
figures and measurements are reproducible.

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [Protein structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein_structure) and [Anfinsen's dogma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anfinsen%27s_dogma)
- RCSB [PDB-101](https://pdb101.rcsb.org/) — short, illustrated explainers on structure and specific proteins, aimed at newcomers

## Comparing proteins in 3D {#sec-s06-compare}

### Sequence alignment versus structure alignment

Session 4 defined an alignment as a hypothesis about which residues
correspond. A **sequence alignment** decides this from the sequences
alone, using substitution scores. A **structure alignment** decides it
from the 3D coordinates, by asking which residues occupy the same
position in the two folds. The notebook compares β-globin both ways with
five proteins, ranging from a close paralog to an unrelated fold:

| Compared with β-globin | Sequence identity\* | Sequence-only score (shuffled max) | Residue pairs agreeing | TM-score |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| α-globin (human, 2HHB) | 43% | 288 (43) | 95% | 0.88 |
| myoglobin (human, 3RGK) | 25% | 111 (46) | 97% | 0.91 |
| neuroglobin (human, 1OJ6) | 22% | 89 (41) | 66% | 0.82 |
| truncated haemoglobin N (*M. tuberculosis*, 1IDR) | 16% | 28 (49) | 0% | 0.57 |
| GFP (jellyfish, 1EMA) | 6% | 25 (50) | — | 0.33 |

: Five proteins compared with β-globin, by sequence and by structure. {#tbl-s06-globins}

\*Identity over the structurally aligned residues. "Sequence-only score"
is the best Smith–Waterman alignment with BLOSUM62, and the number in
brackets is the highest score among 200 alignments against shuffled
versions of the same sequence. "Residue pairs agreeing" is the fraction
of structurally aligned pairs that the sequence alignment also pairs up.
TM-scores are normalised by the length of β-globin.

The table is best read from top to bottom. For α-globin and myoglobin,
the sequence alignment has a strong signal and pairs up almost exactly
the same residues as the structure alignment. (Session 5 showed that
BLAST, with default settings, nevertheless missed myoglobin, because a
heuristic search can skip an alignment that an exhaustive one finds.)
For neuroglobin the sequence signal is still clear, but a third of the
pairs are wrong, because the gaps are in the wrong places. For the
bacterial truncated haemoglobin, the sequence alignment does no better
than shuffled sequences and pairs up none of the right residues. The
structure alignment nevertheless finds a shared globin fold over more
than 100 residues. This is the central lesson: **structure is more
conserved than sequence.** When the sequence evidence fades, structure
can still reveal a relationship.

### Measuring structural similarity: RMSD and TM-score

To compare structures, we need a number for how similar they are.
**RMSD** (root-mean-square deviation) is the most direct measure. It is
the root-mean-square distance between corresponding atoms after the two
structures have been optimally superimposed. RMSD is simple, but it
grows with protein length, and one badly placed loop can inflate it even
when the rest of the fold matches. The **TM-score** avoids these
problems. It weights each residue pair by how close it is, so that small
deviations count fully and large ones hardly at all, and it normalises
by protein length. It runs from 0 to 1 (identical). Unrelated proteins
typically score around 0.2–0.3, and scores above about 0.5 usually mean
the same overall fold. This is a rule of thumb, not a law. The truncated
haemoglobin above (0.57) and GFP (0.33) are clear cases, but scores in
between need other evidence.

### DALI: comparing distance maps

If two proteins have the same fold, their distance maps should look
alike, even when their sequences do not. **DALI** (Holm & Sander, 1993)
uses this idea to compare structures. Rather than superimposing
coordinates, it looks for residue correspondences that make the patterns
of intramolecular distances agree.

![Distance maps of β-globin, human myoglobin and GFP. The first two are
almost indistinguishable although only a quarter of their residues are
identical; GFP's β-barrel gives a completely different pattern.](figs/session06-distance-maps-compared.png){#fig-session06-distance-maps-compared width=100%}

The analogy with sequence alignment is direct:

- Sequence alignment compares residues along two sequences.
- DALI compares patterns of residue–residue geometry.

DALI and **TM-align** (Zhang & Skolnick, 2005), which finds the
superposition that maximises the TM-score, are accurate and still used
for careful pairwise comparisons. They are, however, far too slow to
search hundreds of millions of structures.

### Foldseek: structure search at sequence-search speed

Session 5 ended with MMseqs2, which searches billions of sequences.
**Foldseek** (van Kempen, Steinegger et al., 2024), from the same group,
does the same for structures:

| | Search tool | Searches with |
|---|---|---|
| Sequence (Session 5) | BLAST, MMseqs2 | the amino-acid sequence |
| Structure (this session) | Foldseek | a "structural sequence" |

: Searching by sequence and by structure. {#tbl-s06-search}

The key idea of Foldseek is a change of representation. For each
residue, Foldseek looks at the local 3D environment (the geometry
between that residue and its closest neighbour in space) and assigns one
of 20 discrete structural states, the **3Di alphabet**. A structure thus
becomes a string of 3Di letters, one per residue. Two structures can
then be compared with fast sequence-alignment machinery (the same
prefilter-and-align approach as MMseqs2) instead of expensive geometric
superposition:

```
3D coordinates
   → local geometry around each residue
   → one 3Di state per residue
   → a structural "sequence"
   → fast alignment and database search
```

This makes it possible to search the hundreds of millions of structures
in the AlphaFold Database and the PDB in seconds to minutes. Foldseek is
tens of thousands of times faster than TM-align at comparable
sensitivity.

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Machine-learning preview: a learned representation

Nobody designed the 20 states of Foldseek's 3Di alphabet by hand.
Instead, a machine-learning model (a variational autoencoder) was
trained on pairs of structurally aligned residues to find a compact set
of recurring 3D environments that are conserved between related
structures. You do not need to know how such a model works. The point is
that a *useful representation can itself be learned from data*. In
Session 5, humans chose both the representation (amino acids) and the
scoring scheme (BLOSUM62), whereas in Foldseek, machine learning helped
choose the representation. Sessions 7–12 build up the machinery behind
models that learn increasingly powerful representations.
:::

**A worked comparison.** We ran Foldseek locally on three structures:
the two haemoglobin states used on this page (`2HHB`, deoxy; `1HHO`,
oxy) and green fluorescent protein (`1EMA`). Matching α-to-α or β-to-β
chains between `2HHB` and `1HHO`, which are the *same* protein in two
states, gives a TM-score of **0.98** and an RMSD of **0.7 Å**, about as
similar as two independently solved structures get. α against β globin
(43% identical) still gives a TM-score of **0.90–0.91** (RMSD 1.7–1.8
Å). Searching `2HHB` against GFP, in contrast, returns **no hits**, even
with a loosened significance threshold.

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [Root-mean-square deviation of atomic positions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root-mean-square_deviation_of_atomic_positions) and [Template modeling score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template_modeling_score)
- Foldseek, [GitHub](https://github.com/steineggerlab/foldseek) and [web server](https://search.foldseek.com/search) — try it on any PDB entry or AlphaFold model, no installation needed

## Domains, complexes and conformational states {#sec-s06-states}

### Structural domains

A **domain** is a compact, semi-independent unit of a structure, which
is often able to fold on its own and is reused in many different
proteins. Sessions 3 and 5 met domains from the *sequence* side, as Pfam
families built from profile HMMs. Structural classifications instead
group domains by their 3D shape, which, as the table above showed, can
reveal relationships that sequence misses.

**CATH** (Orengo et al., 1997) classifies domains in four levels:
**C**lass (mainly α, mainly β, α/β, few secondary structures),
**A**rchitecture (the overall arrangement of secondary-structure
elements), **T**opology (how they are connected, that is, the fold), and
**H**omologous superfamily (domains with evidence of common ancestry).
β-globin's domain is `1.10.490.10`: Mainly Alpha → Orthogonal Bundle →
Globin-like → Globins. So are myoglobin, neuroglobin and the *M.
tuberculosis* truncated haemoglobin from the table above. Pfam, which
works from sequence, needs a separate family for the truncated
haemoglobin (PF01152, "Bacterial-like globin", not PF00042, "Globin")
and connects the two only at the level of a *clan*. GFP, in contrast, is
in CATH class 2 (Mainly Beta), Beta Barrel.

Three other classifications exist, each with a different philosophy:
**SCOP** (Murzin et al., 1995; expert manual curation), **ECOD** (Cheng
et al., 2014; organised by evolutionary relationship), and **TED** (Lau,
Bordin et al., 2024; domains parsed automatically from the entire
AlphaFold Database, hundreds of millions of predicted structures). They
do not always agree on where one domain ends or on how distant
superfamilies group together. Knowing that several classifications
exist, and why, therefore matters more than picking one.

### Quaternary structure, interfaces and ligands

Beyond single chains, a complex is held together by **interfaces**,
patches of surface where two chains touch. Interfaces are usually more
hydrophobic and more conserved than the rest of the surface. Many
proteins also bind **ligands**, small molecules or ions such as
haemoglobin's haem groups. Interfaces and ligand-binding sites are where
much of a protein's function happens, and predicting them is one of the
open problems of Session 12.

### One protein, more than one structure: haemoglobin T and R

A PDB entry is one snapshot of one state. Haemoglobin has two classic
states, deoxy (**T**, tense; `2HHB`) and oxy (**R**, relaxed; `1HHO`).
Each chain hardly changes between them (TM-score 0.98), but the two α/β
pairs rotate relative to each other by about 13–15° (Baldwin & Chothia,
1979; the third discussion problem measures it). The notebook measures
one consequence: the distance between the iron atoms of the two β-chain
haems is about 5 Å shorter in the oxy state. This quaternary change is
how haemoglobin binds oxygen cooperatively, since binding at one subunit
makes binding at the others easier.

It follows that **a PDB structure is not necessarily "the" structure of
a protein.** Proteins can occupy different conformational states
depending on ligands, partners and conditions. This matters whenever a
predicted model is compared with "the" experimental structure, and it is
one of the limitations that Session 12 returns to, because AlphaFold
usually predicts one state.

### Further reading

- CATH, [`cathdb.info`](https://www.cathdb.info/); SCOP, [`ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/scop`](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/scop/); ECOD, [`prodata.swmed.edu/ecod`](http://prodata.swmed.edu/ecod/); TED, [`ted.cathdb.info`](https://ted.cathdb.info/)
- RCSB PDB-101, [Hemoglobin](https://pdb101.rcsb.org/motm/41) — the T and R states, illustrated

## From structure back to sequence prediction {#sec-s06-predict}

### Secondary structure as a prediction target

Given only the sequence, could a computer predict which residues become
helix, strand or coil? Stated as a learning problem, the task is:

```
input:   the sequence (or its profile), one window per residue
target:  H (helix), E (strand) or C (coil) for every residue
```

The training labels come from solved structures, assigned by DSSP as in
the notebook. What information could help the prediction? The residue
itself is one source, because some amino acids favour helices, others
strands, and proline and glycine break both. Its neighbours in the
sequence are another. A third, from Session 5, is how that position
varies across homologous sequences, that is, a profile. Sessions 7–11
develop the machinery for learning such mappings, and the course returns
to this problem in Sessions 7, 9 and 10 and in the capstone project.

### Predicting the whole fold

Predicting the full 3D structure has been one of biology's hardest
problems for decades. Since 1994 the **CASP** competition (Critical
Assessment of Structure Prediction) has tested methods blindly, on
structures that are solved but not yet published. The classical
strategies each build on something you have already met:

- **Physics** (*de novo* or *ab initio* modelling) searches for the
  lowest-energy arrangement of the chain, using physical interactions.
  It is rigorous in principle, but so expensive that it long worked only
  for small proteins. **Rosetta** (Baker lab) assembles structures from
  short fragments of known structures, and it grew into a tool for
  protein *design*.
- **Comparative (homology) modelling** finds a related protein of known
  structure (Sessions 4–5) and builds the model on it as a template. It
  is reliable when a template exists, but useless for a new fold. The
  table above shows why it works: related sequences share their
  structure.
- **Evolutionary restraints** use the fact that residues that touch tend
  to mutate together. Large alignments (Session 5) therefore reveal
  which pairs are in contact and fill in a contact map like the one
  above.
- **Deep learning** arrived with AlphaFold2 (2020), which combines
  learned representations, evolutionary information and geometry, and
  was the breakthrough in CASP14. David Baker, Demis Hassabis and John
  Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein design and
  structure prediction. Session 12 covers AlphaFold, once Sessions 7–11
  have built up the neural-network machinery.

In terms of representations, the course's path from here is:

```
sequence
  → profile / evolutionary information      (Session 5)
  → learned representation                  (Sessions 7–11)
  → local structure, contacts, distances    (Sessions 7, 10, 12)
  → 3D structure                            (Session 12)
```

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [Homology modeling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_modeling) and [CASP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CASP)
- Rosetta Commons, [`rosettacommons.org`](https://rosettacommons.org/)

## The course notebook

`notebooks/session06-protein-structure-in-code.ipynb` fetches the two
haemoglobin structures (deoxy `2HHB`, oxy `1HHO`) and makes each level
of structure concrete. It reads the chains and residues from the file,
computes the secondary structure with PyMOL (and compares it with the
PDB annotation that Session 7 uses), and renders an image of the
tetramer. It also draws β-globin's distance and contact maps, builds the
sequence-versus-structure alignment table above, and measures the
iron-to-iron distance that changes by about 5 Å between the two states.
Open it in [Google
Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book/blob/main/notebooks/session06-protein-structure-in-code.ipynb)
via the badge at the top of the notebook page to edit and run it
yourself.

## The lab

**The full lab starts with PyMOL** and uses three structures beyond
haemoglobin. An HIV envelope glycoprotein trimer with an antibody
(`7LXM`) is used for representations, chains, structural alignment
(`cealign`) and finding a sequence inside a structure. A chitinase with
bound metal ions and an inhibitor (`8C6Z`) is used for ligands and
charged residues. Human neuroglobin (`1OJ6`) is used for the central
comparison, which you run with Foldseek in
[`notebooks/session06-lab.ipynb`](https://colab.research.google.com/github/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book/blob/main/notebooks/session06-lab.ipynb):

```
same protein, experimental vs. AlphaFold prediction  → nearly identical
a different globin (hemoglobin)                       → same fold
GFP                                                   → unrelated fold
```

Today, AlphaFold DB simply supplies a structure to inspect, and Session
12 asks how that prediction is produced and how to decide which parts of
it to trust. The lab ends with a structural domain lookup in CATH, and
it shows how to view structures directly in VS Code (the Protein Viewer
extension, which is handy on the course server).

## What's next

This session gave you structural properties that are worth predicting
from sequence. Session 7 starts building the machinery to predict them.
It returns to the weighted sum that a PSSM computes, $S(x) = \sum_i w[i,
x_i]$, and formalises it as a **perceptron** whose weights are *learned*
from labelled examples. It then applies the perceptron to the secondary
structure you met in this session, through Rost & Sander's PHD method, and shows
why the helix you saw in PyMOL can be hard to predict from a window of
residues.
